title: Shopping & Money
subtitle: Numbers, prices, and bargaining
description: From vegetable vendors at HSR to electronics shops on SP Road — count, ask prices, and bargain confidently.

items.context: The first number every Bengaluru newcomer needs — used constantly in prices, quantities, and bus numbering
items.scenario: Telling a vendor you want one piece, or confirming there's only one item left

items.context: Second most used number — pairs with items: eraḍu idli, eraḍu kilo (two kilos) at the vegetable market
items.scenario: Ordering two portions of something, or asking for two pieces from a market stall

items.context: Mūru comes up in addresses, bus routes, and prices — the r sound is longer and rounder than English
items.scenario: Asking for three of something, or telling the auto driver the building number is three

items.context: Nālku has a distinctive ā sound — practice it so vendors understand your quantity request clearly
items.scenario: Buying four items at a market or requesting the 4th floor in a shop

items.context: Aidu is used constantly — five rupees, five pieces, five minutes. One of the most versatile numbers in daily life
items.scenario: Buying five bananas at RS Puram market or asking for five rupees change
items.imageQuery: number five hand gesture five fingers

items.context: The base unit for most small purchases — hattu rupee is still a meaningful amount at local markets and street stalls
items.scenario: Buying a single masal dosa, a bun-butter, or a small snack for around ten rupees
items.imageQuery: ten rupees small purchase india market

items.context: The standard unit when talking about larger purchases — nūru rupees is the typical minimum for most auto rides
items.scenario: Negotiating an auto fare, buying a kilo of vegetables, or asking for a hundred-rupee note back as change

items.context: Sāvira is how prices above a thousand are expressed — rent, mobile recharges, and electronics all go into the sāvira range
items.scenario: Negotiating a monthly PG rent, buying something at a shop, or understanding a quoted price

items.context: Just one word, said with a questioning tone — the most useful thing you'll say at any market or street stall
items.scenario: Pointing at any item without a price tag and asking what it costs — works everywhere from fashion street to vegetable markets
items.imageQuery: how much price asking market stall

items.context: Tumba means very, dubāri means expensive — say this with mild disbelief for best effect. It usually triggers a counter-offer
items.scenario: When a vendor quotes you a clearly inflated price, especially at tourist-adjacent markets or clothing stalls

items.context: Kammi means less, māḍi means make/do — direct, respectful, and universally understood at any negotiable-price situation
items.scenario: After the vendor quotes a price, pause, look doubtful, say this — then wait. Silence is your friend

items.context: Idu means this, koḍi means give — point at what you want and say this. Works when you don't know the item name
items.scenario: Pointing at a specific vegetable, phone case, or food item when you don't know the Kannada name for it

items.english: Do you have another / a different one?
items.context: Bēre means other or different, ide means there is — use it when you want a different colour, size, or variety
items.scenario: When the item you want doesn't fit, isn't the right colour, or you want to see other options first

items.context: Cīla is bag, bēkā is the questioning form of want — a polite question from the vendor. Bags often cost ₹2–₹5 extra
items.scenario: When checking out at a store and the cashier asks if you need a carry bag

items.context: Change (borrowed from English) is universally understood — asking for it firmly but politely is sometimes necessary when vendors claim they have none
items.scenario: After paying with a large note and the vendor seems reluctant to break it — be direct, they usually have change
